newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia new listings hot up as blue-chips cool.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia new listings hot up as blue-chips cool.

text.p: Retail investors have begun turning to new share listings in Malaysia after becoming disenchanted by lagging blue chips, and analysts see the trend continuing in the medium-term.

The revival of small-capitalised issues on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange (KLSE) was boosted by the return of trading syndicates who took losses in the past few months after the central bank announced measures to curb credit, they said.

"I think there are syndicates behind these stocks," said Patrick Lim, president of the Malaysian Investors Association. "Otherwise, with the general market weak, how can new listings command a premium to those already listed?"
One newly-listed share, lingerie maker Audrey International (Malaysia) Bhd, triggered a stock exchange trading limit at its market debut, a rare occurrence.

Audrey opened trading on July 3 at 10.00 ringgit ($4.00), five times above its offer price of 2.00 ringgit. Potential buyers of the stock could only make further purchases if its price fell below 10.00 that day. It ended on Friday at 9.10 ringgit.

Analysts said prices of small-cap issues are easy to push higher due to the limited number of shares available to the public. A typical small company listing on the Second Board floats about only a quarter of its issued and paid-up share capital to the public.
"They are easy to push. It's difficult to push up main board shares," said an institutional dealer at K&N Kenanga stock brokerage.

Other Second Board stocks that have captured gains in heavy trading in the past few weeks include furniture maker Len Cheong Holding Bhd and toiletries producer Zaitun Bhd. Len Cheong listed on June 20 at 6.30 ringgit.
Zaitun was placed under trading restrictions on June 18 after its share price surged on apparent speculative buying. It listed on June 13 at 6.55 ringgit and ended on Friday at 11.80.
Trading syndicates -- individuals who group together to push up selected stocks -- are thought to be actively involved in boosting some of the shares, though nobody can say who exactly they are.
In contrast, institutional investors have been taking a lukewarm attitude toward Kuala Lumpur blue-chip stocks on concerns over still-firm interest rates and slower corporate earnings growth.
The March announcement by the central Bank Negara on credit curbs for property purchases also exposed worries of a property glut and started the share market's slide, analysts said.
From its peak of 1,270.67 points on February 28, the index of 100 large-capitalised issues on Friday ended at 1,073.31, 197.36 points or 15.53 percent below its highest level so far.
"Interest rates are still quite firm. There's nothing much to tell my clients," said an equity sales manager at a Japanese brokerage in Singapore.
Other regional markets are also in vogue, attracting investors away from Malaysia. "The action now is in Hong Kong and Thailand," said Gan Kim Khoon, research manager at SocGen-Crosby.

In Kuala Lumpur, analysts said the trend is likely to continue in the medium-term. "For the next two, three months people are going for the speculatives, that's the trend we see," said the K&N Kenanga dealer.

Demand to list Second Board shares also continued to be hot. A KLSE official said out of 38 companies listed on the exchange so far this year, 26 or two-thirds were headed for the smaller-capitalised sector.
